list.listitem: Consider a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis (UC) in patients who present with intermittent bloody diarrhea, rectal urgency and tenesmus; confirm the diagnosis with colonoscopy with biopsies. C
Initially treat mild to moderate non-extensive UC using topical 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA). A
Initially treat mild to moderate extensive UC using topical 5-ASA and high dose oral 5-ASA. B
Patients who fail to respond to 5-ASA compounds may require steroid therapy; those who fail steroid therapy may need anti-TNF therapy or vedolizumab.B
Patients with UC are at higher risk for colorectal cancer; perform screening colonoscopies at regular intervals. B
Refer the following patients to a surgeon for colectomy: those with toxic megacolon, perforation, or massive hemorrhage or those who fail to respond to maximal medical therapy. C

background.definition: UC is a chronic disease characterized by diffuse mucosal inflammation of the colon. It always involves the rectum and may extend proximally in a contiguous pattern.

list.listitem: The highest annual incidence of UC was 24.3 per 100,000 person-years in Europe,19.2 per 100,000 person-years in North America, and 6.3 per 100,000 person-years in Asia and the Middle East.

Sex differences were inconsistent, suggesting that the disease occurred equally among both sexes. Universally, incidence rates for both CD and UC were highest among the second to the fourth decade of life.
$500,000,000 lost in productivity per year.
Precise etiology unknown.
The current hypothesis involves primary dysregulation of the colonic mucosal immune system leading to excessive immunologic response to normal microflora.
Consider a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis (UC) in patients who present with intermittent bloody diarrhea, rectal urgency and tenesmus; confirm the diagnosis with colonoscopy with biopsies. C
Order stool studies to search for ova and parasites and Clostridium difficile toxin to exclude an infectious etiology. C
An elevated fecal calprotectin level suggests IBD and is useful in guiding when to refer a primary care patient to GI. C
The role of blood tests to differentiate UC from Crohn's disease is currently not known. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Perianal lesions less common; frank bleeding less common than in UC
Occurs in older patients with vascular disease; sudden onset; often painful
Sudden onset; pathogens present in stool; pain may be a predominant feature
History of recent antibiotic use; Clostridium difficile toxin in stool
Meets Rome II criteria for irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)

list.listitem: UC typically presents with intermittent bloody diarrhea, rectal urgency, and tenesmus.

Extraintestinal manifestations include: arthritis (5%-10%), deep vein thrombosis (0.3%), primary sclerosing cholangitis (3%), pulmonary embolism (0.2%), pyoderma gangrenosum (0.5%-2%), oral ulcerations (10%), osteoporosis (15%), and uveitis (0.5%-3%).
Clubbing in a patient with bowel symptoms is a specific sign for UC if present in a patient with bowel symptoms; absence of clubbing does not rule out UC.
See the guidelines in for assessing disease severity.

Colonoscopy with biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis of UC, with a reported 99% sensitivity for diagnosing colonic pathology in patients with diarrhea. If the terminal ileum is normal, upper endoscopy to evaluate the stomach and duodenum or imaging are not needed unless symptoms suggest upper GI tract involvement.
Stool testing to rule out clostriodes difficile as the cause of symptoms is recommended by 2019 ACG guidelines, including in patients hospitalized with severe UC.
Blood tests to differentiate UC from Crohn's disease (pANCA and ASCA) are specific, but not sensitive for differentiating UC from Crohn's disease and are not routinely recommended.

A 2018 study out of China showed that a combination of any 2 of 3 serological markers may increase the accuracy and ability to diagnose Crohn’s disease. These markers include anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibody (ASCA IgA), anti-mannobioside carbohydrate antibody (AMCA) and anti-chitobioside carbohydrate antibody (ACCA). This has a sensitivity and specific of >75%. Presence of a single antibody was insufficient for diagnosis.
However, the 2019 ACG guidelines recommend against using serologic antibody testing to diagnose UC or to determine prognosis.
An elevated fecal calprotectin level suggests IBD and is useful in guiding when to refer a primary care patient to GI, but does not differentiate between UC and Crohn's disease.

A 2018 prospective observational cohort study showed that fecal calprotectin levels >782 ug/g of stool can be used to differentiate acute severe colitis from mild to moderate UC with a sensitivity of 84% and a specificity of 88%.

Fecal calprotectin is recommended by 2019 ACG guidelines to determine severity of disease and to evaluate response to treatment in patients with active UC whereas fecal immunochemical test (FIT) may be an appropriate surrogate test for mucosal healing and to monitor for recurrence.
Fecal calprotectin is also currently the most promising predictive marker for recurrence in UC and may be used for monitoring, but it lacks an accurate cut-off value.

In a study published January 2023, it was shown that neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) levels were significantly increased at diagnosis and active disease of childhood IBD and can be a non-invasive inflammatory biomarker that should be used in the initial evaluation and follow-up of the disease activity in children.
Consider UC in patients with intermittent bloody diarrhea.
Stool studies for ova and parasites, culture, and Clostridium difficile toxin are useful to exclude other causes of colitis.
Colonoscopy or proctosigmoidoscopy with biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis of UC.
See for assessment of disease severity and for treatment recommendations.
Initially treat mild to moderate non-extensive UC using topical 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA). Treat UC proctitis using rectal 5-ASA at a dose of 1 g/d. A
Initially treat mild to moderate extensive UC using topical 5-ASA and high dose oral 5-ASA. B
Response to 5-ASA compounds is dose dependent; based upon cost, side effects, and effectiveness, 5-ASA compounds are the preferred first-line oral treatment. B
Nonpathogenic E. coli Nissle 1917 may be as effective in the treatment and remission of UC as 5-ASA products. B
Consider oral or IV steroid therapy for patients who do not respond to 5-ASA compounds. C

Patients who do not respond to IV steroids are candidates for immunomodulator therapy. Intravenous infliximab is effective in inducing remission in refractory UC, but is associated with an increased risk of anaphylaxis and infections. Vedolizumab is another novel treatment option. A
Refer to 2019 ACG guidelines summarized below to guide therapy.B
See for guidance with regards to assessing severity, and for dosing of commonly used drugs in milder disease.

Agents are classified for induction and maintenance of remission in patients with moderate to severe UC based on magnitude of effect (small, moderate or large) and certainty of evidence (low, moderate or high): Large magnitude of effect, moderate to high certainty: upadacitinib, tofacitinib Moderate magnitude of effect, moderate to high certainty: mesalazine, ozanimod, risankizumab Small magnitude of effect, moderate to high certainty: etrasimod, vedolizumab, infliximab Low certainty: filgotinib, golimumab, mirikizumab, ustekinumab
All patients with UC should receive recombinant zoster vaccination, annual flu vaccine, and pneumococcal vaccination with a booster at 5 year.

listitem.strong: Induction of remission for mildly active UC

list.listitem: First line therapy is rectal 5-ASA compounds 1 gm/day, or oral 5-ASA 2 gm/day for more extensive disease.
Oral budesonide 9 mg/day is recommended for patients not responsive to 5-ASA.
There is no evidence that changing to a different 5-ASA or using higher doses such as 4.8 gm/day are effective.

listitem.strong: Maintenance of remission with previous mildly active UC

list.listitem: First line therapy is rectal 5-ASA 1 gm/day.
If extensive disease, oral 5-ASA 2 gm/day is recommended. Guidelines recommend against using oral corticosteroids for maintenance of remission.
Induction of remission for moderately to severely active UC:
First line therapy is oral budesonide or other oral systemic corticosteroids.

Anti-tumor necrosis factor (TNF) therapy with adalimumab, golimumab, or infliximab are also recommended as treatment options. If anti-TNF therapy is needed, adding 5-ASA is not recommended. Infliximab should be used in combination with a thiopurine.
Vedolizumab and tofacitinib can also be used for induction of remission, and following failed anti-TNF therapy.
In patients who initially responded to an anti-TNF drug but are now losing response, consider checking drug levels.
Guidelines recommend against monotherapy with thiopurines or methotrexate. A Cochrane review found no evidence for methotrexate for induction of remission of UC.

listitem.strong: Maintenance of remission in patients with previous moderate to severe UC

list.listitem: If induction was successful using corticosteroids, thiopurines are recommended to maintain remission.
After anti-TNF induction, continue using anti-TNF therapy to maintain remission.
After vedolizumab induction, continue using vedolizumab to maintain remission.
After tofacitinib induction, continue using tofacitinib to maintain remission.

Guidelines recommend against using systemic steroids or methotrexate to maintain remission, or using concomitant 5-ASA in addition to anti-TNF therapy. A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for methotrexate for maintenance of remission of UC.

listitem.strong: Hospitalized patients with acute severe UC

list.listitem: Provide DVT prophylaxis and test for C. difficile infection. If c. difficile is present, vancomycin rather than metronidazole is recommend.
Total parenteral nutrition is recommended, but routine use of broad spectrum antibiotics is not.
Treat with systemic corticosteroids, 60 mg/day of methylprednisolone or hydrocortisone 100 mg tid to qid

If steroids do not induce remission within 3 to 5 days, start infliximab or cyclosporine. If remission is achieved with infliximab continue it, if it is achieved with cyclosporine, maintain remission with a thiopurine or vedolizumab.

A trial randomized 64 patients hospitalized with acute severe UC who responded to steroids to azathioprine + infliximab with a 7 day steroid taper or to azathioprine with a longer tapering regiment. At one year, treatment failure had occurred more often in the azathioprine only arm (81% vs 53%, p = 0.03, NNH = 3).

listitem.strong: Individual clinical trials and systematic reviews

list.listitem: A systematic review of 5-ASA compounds identified 7 RCTs with 2745 patients that compared once daily dosing with more frequent dosing. Relapse rates were no lower with more frequent dosing.

A 2019 meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials found that once daily dosing of mesalazine was safe and as effective as twice daily dosing for mild-to-moderate active US. Once daily dosing was effective in clinical and endoscopic remission.
Sulfasalazine is as effective as other 5-ASA compounds but may not be as well tolerated.

A systematic review compared oral vs. topical vs. combined 5-ASA therapy for patients with active UC and found combined 5-ASA therapy appeared superior to oral 5-ASAs for induction of remission of mildly to moderately active UC. Intermittent topical 5-ASAs appeared superior to oral 5-ASAs for preventing relapse of quiescent UC.
For patients who do not respond to 5-ASA compounds, give oral prednisone, 40 to 60 mg/d, for 10 to 14 days.
Parenteral methotrexate was not superior to placebo in preventing relapses of UC in patients who achieved steroid-free response during induction therapy.
If the disease does not respond to oral steroids, consider hospitalization and IV steroids; if IV steroids fail, treat UC with immunomodulating drugs, such as cyclosporine or infliximab.

In a meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials, corticosteroid use was associated with higher biologic response rates for UC during the induction phase, but were not associated with improved maintenance of remission.

A network meta-analysis identified 28 trials with 12,504 patients comparing drugs for moderate to severe UC. It concluded that upadacitinib 45 mg once daily was most likely to achieve clinical remission (P-score 0.98) followed by infliximab 5 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg. Upadacitinib was ranked first both in patients who had previously been exposed to anti-TNF drugs and those who had not.

In an individual participant data (IPD) pooled analysis of trials of infliximab and golimumab, results suggest that patients with moderate-severe UC who are escalated to anti-TNF therapy, continuing 5-ASA does NOT improve clinical outcomes.

A systematic review and meta-analysis in 2018 found that infliximab and cyclosporine are both therapies able to treat acute severe ulcerative colitis refractory to steroids. It found no difference in efficacy between the two treatments in both short term and long term results.

Vedolizumab (Enyvio) is a novel therapy approved for treatment of UC. It is a humanized monoclonal antibody to alpha-4 beta-7 integrin. An RCT randomized 769 patients with active moderately severe UC to vedolizumab or adalimumab for one year. At the end of one year, more patients in the vedolizumab group had achieved clinical remission (31.3% vs 22.5%, p = 0.006, NNT = 11). On the other hand, steroid free remission occurred less often in the vedolizumab group (12.6% vs 21.8%, NNT = 11).

In an RCT, treatment with abrilumab (an anti-alpha-4 beta-7 antibody) resulted in significant remission, response and mucosal healing rates versus placebo. The data reaffirms the targeting of the alpha-4 beta-7 pathway for UC treatment. This short term study did not fully assess treatment effects beyond 8 weeks.

Mirkizumab was studied in two randomized placebo-controlled trials, one for induction and if a response, to a second maintenance trial. Clinical remission at week 12 occurrred more often in the induction trial (24% vs 13%, p < 0.001, NNT = 9) and at week 40 in the maintenance trial (50% vs 25%, p < 0.001, NNT = 4).
Tulisokibart is a TNF like cytokine monoclonal antibody for moderate to severe UC. It was more effective than placebo in inducing clinical remission (26% vs 1%, p < 0.001, NNT = 4).

Based on high-certainty evidence, a Cochrane review concluded that oral tofacitinib is more effective than placebo at inducing clinical and endoscopic remission at 52 weeks among patients with moderate to severe UC who demonstrated clinical response after 8 weeks of induction therapy with tofacitinib 10mg twice daily. Adverse events to tofacitinib were similar to placebo.

An RCT randomized 645 patients with moderate to severe active UC to ozanimod (a selective sphingosine-1-phophate receptor modulator) or placebo for 10 weeks to evaluate induction, and were then rerandomized at 10 weeks and reevaluated for maintenance efficacy at one year. ozanimod was effective for both induction (clinical remission 18.4% vs 6%, p < 0.001, NNT = 8) and maintenance (37% vs 18.5%, p < 0.005, NNT = 5).

Etrasimod, a once-daily, oral, sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) receptor modulator was effective and well tolerated as an induction and maintenance therapy in patients with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis.

A Cochrane review concluded that tacrolimus, based on low certainty evidence, may be more effective than placebo and may be comparable to beclomethasone for inducing clinical remission or clinical improvement in corticosteroid-refractory colitis or proctitis.

A Cochrane review of 12 RCTs found no benefit for antibiotics for the induction of remission at the end of the trial period, but some benefit for inducing remission and improving clinical response at 12 months compared to placebo. Longer trials are recommended before stronger conclusions can be made.
A study of 105 patients with mild to moderately active UC found that rosiglitazone 4 mg twice daily for 12 weeks increased the likelihood of clinical response and remission more than placebo.

There is some evidence that low-molecular-weight heparin administered in extended colon-release tablets improves clinical remission and improvement in patients with mild to moderate disease. Subcutaneous low molecular-weight heparin or unfractionated heparin have no benefit.

Nonpathogenic E. coli Nissle 1917 may be as effective in the treatment and maintenance of ulcerative colitis as 5-ASA products. A Cochrane review found low-certainty evidence for the efficacy of probiotics for induction of remission in UC. However, more studies regarding the efficacy of probiotics in maintenance of remission of UC are needed to draw definite conclusions. Additionally, a Cochrane review found no additional benefit from prebiotics (and it may even increase adverse events) as an adjuvant treatment for UC to prevent clincal relapse compared to placebo, based on very low certainty evidence.
Consider colectomy for severe symptoms that do not respond to maximal medical therapy or to complications of ulcerative colitis, such as massive hemorrhage, perforation, or toxic megacolon.
Among women with infertility, the effects of surgical therapy for IBD are uncertain, based on a Cochrane review.
The risk of postoperative infectious complications from medical therapies for IBD remains unclear, according to a Cochrane review of 68 trials.
If possible stop or reduce dose of steroids prior to surgery, and provide medical prophylaxis against thromboembolism.

An SR that included 39 RCTs involving 3204 patients, suggested that Kangfuxin liquid (KFXL) combined with ASA has good therapeutic effect for UC and might be a safe approach in managing UC. More high-quality, multicenter randomized, double-blind trials with a large sample size are required to generate a high level of clinical evidence.

A meta-analysis with relatively low sample size showed that Trichuris suis ova therapy had no statistical benefit for IBD patients, suggesting clinicians should consider its value carefully before putting into clinical practice.

A meta-analysis of 22 low-quality RCTs (n = 2028) comparing the herbal medicine Gegen Qinlian Decoction (GQD), alone or in combination with traditional Western UC therapies, with Western medicine alone suggested potential benefits and fewer harms.

Omega-3 fatty acids are not useful in treatment or maintenance of remission of ulcerative colitis. Acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) is a psychological intervention that comprises acceptance and mindfulness procedures and strategies. In a small RCT of patients with IBD, an 8-week ACT therapy course improved stress symptoms, assessed with the Depression Anxiety Stress scale.
A Cochrane review concluded no firm conclusions can be made regarding the effectiveness of vitamin D for the treatment of IBD, given the very low certainty of evidence from RCTs.
A Cochrane review found uncertain evidence for the efficacy of cannabis for the treatment of UC.

Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) increased clinical remission in a pooled analysis of 2 RCTs and 8 cohort studies and a subsequent RCT, but more studies are needed to establish long-term benefits. The 2023 Rome consensus conference concluded that while FMT maybe effective for inducing remission in patients with UC, it should only be used in the context of randomized trials at the current time.

In a randomised controlled trial, multidonor faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) with anti-inflammatory diet effectively induced deep remission in mild-moderate UC which was sustained with anti-inflammatory diet over 1 year.

A Cochrane review found low-certainty evidence for the efficacy of FMT in the induction of clinical and endoscopic remission for UC, and very low-certainty evidence that FMT is effective for maintenance of remission in UC.

In another RCT on fecal microbiota (FMT), there is evidence that a short course and low intensity treatment (3-dose, 1-week induction course) of pooled donor stool FMT was more like to induce clinical and endoscopic remission in participants with active UC at 8 weeks compared to autologous FMT. Other previous studies have high treatment burden that would likely limit clinical applicability. As with other studies, further research is needed to assess longer term maintenance of remission and safety.

In another FMT study in patients with active UC, specific bacteria (Eubacterium hallii, Rosburia inulivorans) and metabolic pathways (increased levels of short chain fatty acids, bile acids biosynthesis) were associated with induction of remission. These findings may be of value in the design of microbe-based therapies.
A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for the efficacy of adjuvant treatment with antidepressants for managing IBD.
Based on a Cochrane review, there is uncertainty in the effects of dietary interventions for induction and remission in UC.

Another Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for different interventions to manage abdominal pain in ulcerative colitis, including dietary interventions (eg, low FODMAP diet, kefir diet), relaxation training, yoga, and stellate ganglion block.
Similarly, interventions to treat fatigue in IBD have uncertain effects, based on a Cochrane review.
Hospitalize patients who do not respond to oral medical therapy or who develop complications of UC.
UC is usually co-managed with a gastroenterologist, especially if immunomodulator drugs are used. Refer to a general or colorectal surgeon if surgical therapy is anticipated.
Toxic megacolon, defined as dilation of the transverse colon to greater than 5.5 cm, is indicative of fulminant disease and is a true surgical emergency requiring immediate surgical consultation.

Intravenous (ie, ferric carboxymaltose) and oral iron (ie, ferric maltol) are effective in treating iron-deficiency anemia in IBD, based on a Cochrane review of 11 RCTs. Intravenous iron appears more effective than oral iron, with NNT = 11. Conclusions regarding safety cannot be made given very low certainty of evidence.
The Toronto Consensus Statement on the treatment of hospitalized adults with severe UC makes several recommendations based on an iterative, evidence-based process:
Initial evaluation should include stool samples for C. difficile, abdominal radiographys, flexible sigmoidoscopy to assess severity, and assessment for risk of TB (in case infliximab is needed).
TPN should be avoided, and patients should preferentially receive a normal diet or enteral nutrition.
Consider thromboembolic prophylaxis, and avoid routine use of antibiotics or narcotic pain relievers.

First line therapy is with IV corticosteroids; consider early escalation to infliximab or cyclosporine when parenteral steroids have failed (after 72 hours). Assess response to infliximab or cyclosporine at 5 to 7 days. If on IV cyclosporine and good response, switch to oral cyclosporine. Patients responding to an initial dose of infliximab should receive subsequent induction doses at 2 and 6 weeks, followed by maintenance infliximab therapy.
If possible, admit patient to a center with experience in these patients and use of these drugs.
Surgery is an option when parenteral steroids fail, and should be considered when second-linemedical therapy fails and in the patient with complications.
UC increases the risk of colorectal cancer; order screening colonoscopies routinely after a diagnosis of UC. B
More severe UC is more difficult to treat. B.

Patients who are young at initial diagnosis (< 40 years), who have extensive disease, severe endoscopic disease, or who are hospitalized for colitis have a worse prognosis. This is also true of patients with lower serum albumin or higher c-reactive protein. B

In cohort of 1515 Danish patients with UC who were followed for up to 30 years after diagnosis, there was no increased overall risk of cancer compared to background incidence rates, despite higher risks in men of colorectal cancer (standardized incidence ratio [SIR], 2.43; 95% CI 1.05-4.78) and prostate cancer (SIR 1.82; 95% CI 1.17-2.71).
UC increases the patient's risk of developing colon cancer (2% in the first 10 years, 8% in the first 20 years, and 18% in the first 30 years).
Order screening colonoscopies for patients with UC 8 years after a diagnosis of pancolitis and 12 to 15 years after a diagnosis of left-sided colitis.
Order subsequent colonoscopies every 2 to 3 years.

Surveillance colonoscopies can reduce development of colorectal cancer by 42% and colorectal cancer associated a death by 62% in those with IBD. Prognosis is improved with detection of early stage cancers.

In patients with UC, noninvasive biomarkers, including fecal calprotectin, fecal lactoferrin, and serum CRP can inform disease monitoring and management. (American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) guideline).

Small prospective study showed significant improvement in qulaity of life and overall satisfaction with the use of telemedicine platform during follow up appointments in patients with IBD. However, a Cochrane review did not find clinically meaningful differences in patient-oriented outcomes between remote care through telehealth versus standard care for adults with IBD.
Instruct patients to take all prescribed medications in order to prevent relapses of UC that may result in hospitalization and/or complications.
Advise patients to undergo screening colonoscopy as recommended to screen for colon cancer.

Patient education, added to standard care, does not appear to improve patient-oriented outcomes in UC, but the Cochrane reviewers recommended caution in intepreting these findings given the lack of clear information in the components of education or standard care in the included trials.

feature.caption: Drugs for Treatment of Ulcerative Colitis.
feature.feature_body:
Preparation Delivery Site Usual Dosing
Oral agents
Pro-drugs converted to 5-ASA in the colon
Sulfasalazine (Azulfidine, 500mg) Colon 3-6 g/d (acute)
2-4 g/d (maintenance)
Olsalazine (Dipentum, 250 mg) Colon 1-3 g/d
Balsalazide (Colazal, 750 mg) Colon 6.75 g/d
Delayed release
Mesalamine (Asacol, 400 mg, 800 mg) Distal ileum-colon 2.4-4.8 g/d (acute)
0.8-4.8 g/d (maintenance)
(Claversal,* Mesasal,* Salofalk,* 250 mg, 500 mg) Ileum-colon 1.5-3.0 g/d (acute)
0.75-3.0 g/d (maintenance)
Sustained release
Mesalamine Stomach-colon 2-4 g/d (acute)
(Pentasa, 250 mg, 500 mg, 1,000 mg*)
1.5-4.0 g/d (maintenance)
Intravenous
Vedolizumab (Entyvio) Gut 300 mg IV every 4-8 weeks
Rectal agents Rectal drugs
Mesalamine suppository Rectum 1.0-1.5 g/d (acute)
(Canasa, 400 mg,* 500 mg, 1,000 mg*)
500-1,000 mg/d (maintenance)
Mesalamine enema Rectum-splenic flexure 1-4 g/d (acute)
(Rowasa, 1 g,* 4 g)
1 g daily-1 g three times a week (maintenance)
* Not available in the United States. From Langan RC, Gotsch PB, Krafczyk MA, Skillinge DD. Ulcerative colitis: diagnosis and treatment. Am Fam Physician 2007;76:9.
